analysis.investment_thesis: Davin Sons Retail fails the Magic Formula on the quality axis — ROE of 0.15% implies near-zero return on capital, which disqualifies it regardless of valuation. A P/E of 12 on a ₹17.8 Cr micro-cap incorporated only in 2022 is not "cheap enough" to offset a non-existent economic engine.
key_strengths: P/E of 12 is not egregiously expensive in absolute terms
Promoter holding of 49.68% shows reasonable skin-in-the-game
Operates in two large TAMs (FMCG wholesale + apparel)
key_risks: ROE of 0.15% indicates effectively no return on capital — fails Magic Formula quality gate
Incorporated 2022 — no 3-year ROIC track record to validate the business
₹17.8 Cr micro-cap in commoditized wholesale/garments — no pricing power or moat
red_flags: ROE 0.15% is a near-zero profitability signal — EBIT likely razor-thin
Brand-new entity (2022) with unproven earnings power; P/E could be driven by a one-time blip
Wholesale FMCG + garments is a low-margin, capital-cycling business — poor ROIC structurally
analysis.detailed_analysis:
The Magic Formula ranks companies on two axes: earnings yield (cheap?) and return on capital (good?). Davin Sons fails catastrophically on the second. A reported ROE of 0.15% means shareholder capital is earning essentially nothing — even if we charitably assume ROIC is modestly higher than ROE, this is nowhere near the >20% threshold I require. The P/E of 12 translates to an earnings yield of ~8%, which is acceptable but not a bargain, and certainly not enough to compensate for a business that doesn't compound capital.

Structurally, a two-year-old micro-cap (₹17.8 Cr) straddling FMCG wholesale and ready-made garments is exactly the kind of low-barrier, low-margin operation where high ROIC is nearly impossible to sustain. Without an EBIT track record spanning 3+ years, any quality signal is noise. This is a hard pass on the systematic framework — cheap is not enough; it must also be good, and this one isn't.
